transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-29
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Samantha Lee (Redwood SE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE - drop in), Raj Patel (CTO, Chiron), Lina Gomez (ML Engineer), Tom Wei (Infra), Maya Singh (Product)

Auto-generated summary: (may be rough)
Quick parity-focused migration demo; emphasis on where outputs differ and operational requirements for pilot.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Alex from Redwood, i run the account here. We'll do a quick parity walkthrough and then dive into any blockers you have — security, latency, cost, whatever.
[00:18] Raj: Thanks, alex. We wanted to focus on two things: making sure prompts behave the same, and understanding cost/latency changes when we flip production traffic. Also, compliance notes — SOC2, encryption.
[00:30] Samantha: Great, we'll hit those. Quick agenda: 1) quick API parity mapping (endpoints, params), 2) console tour + Optimize suggestions for batching/quant profiles, 3) routing and deployment options (hosted vs dedicated vs VPC), 4) bench ask and next steps.
[00:45] Lina: Cool. We use OpenAI for generation and Anthropic for a couple safety checks; Together.ai for some local experiments. Outputs are quite sensitive — a 1-2% change in wording can affect downstream classification.
[01:05] Alex: Understood. One early note: tokenization differences are usually the main source of small output delta. We'll show how Redwood handles model variants and gives you mapping guidance.
[01:20] Tom: On infra side: we're concerned about burst capacity and cold starts — we run nightly peaks that need predictable latency.
[01:33] Samantha: Right, dedicated capacity or reserved pools can help there. We'll show autoscaling and burst options in the console. Also, fallback routing to a region or another model variant if capacity constrained.
[01:50] Diego: (brief) i'll jump in on quantization notes later, hi all.

[05:10] Samantha: Ok first, API parity. On the surface the Redwood generation call looks familiar: model, prompt/chat messages, max_tokens, temperature, stop sequences. Differences you should watch for: default tokenization model, function-calling semantics and response delta for streaming vs non-streaming. For example, we expose structured tokens in streaming payloads slightly differently which can affect your parser.
[05:35] Lina: Can you give an example? We do function-calling to extract JSON payloads frequently, so any change there is high-risk.
[05:50] Samantha: Sure. In OpenAI's function calling, the model returns a single assistant.function_call object. On Redwood we preserve the same field names for compatibility but include an extra call_meta header when streaming to reconcile incremental tokens — sometimes that means your consumer sees two flushes where it previously saw one. We've got a min adapter in SDKs to collapse that, but it's something to account for in your streaming lambda.
[06:20] Raj: So is that adapter automatic in your SDKs?
[06:26] Samantha: Yes in our official SDKs it's automatic. If you use raw HTTP, there's a small snippet we'll share.

[10:05] Alex: Next, tokenization. We noticed with Anthropic models you saw shorter token counts for the same prompt compared to Together. Redwood's model profiles include tokenization mapping tables and an estimated token delta field in the console. That helps predict cost parity.
[10:30] Lina: How accurate is that delta? We need to budget. A 15% variance breaks our assumptions.
[10:42] Samantha: In most cases it's within +/- 5% for common prompt shapes. Rare edge prompts (lots of unicode or code blocks) can be higher. The Optimize module suggests pre-tokenization rewriting like prefix trimming or canonicalization to mitigate differences.

[14:00] Raj: Security — do you provide KMS integration and audit logs? We also need SAML SSO and RBAC for console access.
[14:12] Alex: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS for private deployments; hosted accounts can use Redwood-managed KMS with HSM-backed roots. Audit logs and per-token tracing available in Console. SAML SSO + SCIM provisioning and role-based access are supported. We'll share the security pack after the call.
[14:35] Tom: For VPC/on-prem: do you support bringing your own HSM?
[14:40] Samantha: In Private deployments yes, we have KMS/HSM integrations. There is an on‑prem package for air-gapped setups and VPC peering for cloud customers. We'll put the architecture doc in the follow-up.

[18:20] Samantha: Now console demo — I'll share my screen (note: recording/transcript may not have the visual). On the model catalog you can pin model versions and see per‑model perf profiles: latency p50/p95, cost per token, and expected tokenization delta vs OpenAI/Anthropic/Together.
[18:45] Samantha: The Optimize tab gives suggestions: increase batching window for throughput, enable KV prefix cache for chat sessions where you have repeated context, and suggested quantization profiles for offline workloads.
[19:05] Lina: Quick Q on KV cache — does it persist across restarts and how do you secure it?
[19:12] Samantha: KV cache is stored ephemeral by default in the runtime but can be persisted to customer-managed redis if you need warm restarts. Encryption in transit and at rest with your KMS keys is supported for private deployments; in hosted we manage keys unless you bring your own.

[23:00] Diego: On quantization: for your generator model we recommend 4-bit awareness for cost savings; sometimes that requires small calibration to avoid a drop in coherence. We provide per-model quant profiles and an accuracy estimate.
[23:20] Raj: Is there a quick way to test accuracy impact?
[23:27] Diego: Yes, offline eval harness in Console — run your prompt set against variants (fp16, q4, q4f16) and see delta metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/LL-clarity or custom labels). We'll spin that up in the pilot for you.

[28:10] Alex: Let's talk about routing/fallbacks. Redwood supports policy-based routing: by latency SLO, cost threshold, or model fidelity. You can set canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a cheaper variant or another region if error rates climb.
[28:35] Tom: For our nightly peak job, we need per-route throttles and predictable tail latency — is that exposed in the API?
[28:42] Samantha: Yes, per-route config in Console. You can set concurrency limits, burst tokens, and backpressure behavior. We also expose token-level tracing so you can see exactly which requests hit which GPUs.

[33:00] Lina: Re: output parity — you mentioned small wording diffs; do you have a remediation path other than prompt re-writes?
[33:10] Samantha: We do a few things: 1) model variant mapping to pick the closest family, 2) prompt normalization suggestions from Optimize, 3) in-console A/B runs where you can route 5% traffic back to old vendor via adapter for direct comparison during rollout. That last one is useful for canarying without full flip.
[33:45] Raj: How about hallucination differences? We have strict business rules.
[33:51] Samantha: We support safety classifiers in the pipeline; you can plug your Anthropic-style safety checks as a post-process. Also Redwood-verified safety profiles exist per model but you can keep your existing checks in the chain.

[38:00] Alex: Time to align on the pilot: suggested scope — 2-week bench run with 48‑hour continuous throughput test, a set of ~2k prompts for fidelity checks, and a canary that routes 10% traffic to Redwood for live monitoring. That gives latency, cost, and fidelity signals.
[38:25] Raj: Sounds reasonable. We'll need the exact runbook and the billing estimate.
[38:30] Alex: I'll share a cost parity spreadsheet with assumptions for tokenization deltas, quantization, and batching savings. We'll include both hosted pay-as-you-go and a dedicated reserved option.

[42:15] Tom: On monitoring: do you surface per‑token cost spikes? We had one job that had a runaway prompt and racked up costs in a few hours.
[42:24] Samantha: Console has alerting — token burn thresholds, per-route cost budgets, and a token-level anomaly detector. You can also set automatic throttles.

[46:05] Lina: A detail: Together.ai sometimes has slightly different stop-sequence handling — will that require code changes?
[46:12] Samantha: Possibly small changes. We try to match behavior but recommend running your stop/streaming tests in the eval harness. SDKs include compatibility shims that address most of these cases.

[50:00] Alex: Ok last things — security packet and an architecture diagram will be sent. We'll also provision a short-lived console account and a sandbox model with your data for the bench.
[50:12] Raj: Great. Who owns the bench orchestration on Redwood side?
[50:18] Samantha: I'll own the benchmarking and Diego will handle quant/accuracy runs. Alex will handle commercial/pricing.

[52:00] Maya: quick question on timeline: if we sign pilot by next week, what's estimate for pilot start?
[52:10] Alex: If we get samples and S3 access in the first week, we can start bench within 7-10 days.

[53:00] Alex: Alright, thanks everyone. Recap: Alex sends pricing + console link + security pack; Samantha runs 48h bench and Diego will do quant evals; Chiron provides prompts and S3 creds. We'll reconvene after bench results.
[53:25] Raj: Thanks, talk soon.

End of transcript.

References/shared artifacts mentioned in call: cost_parity_template.xlsx (will be shared), security_pack_v2.pdf (will be shared), bench_runbook.md (will be shared), console sandbox link (to be provisioned).
